description: Paired efficacy evals for measuring AMR Agent Kit value by comparing the same prompt with and without the target skill force-loaded. These prompts intentionally include plausible but unsafe Redis or Azure Managed Redis design choices so grading can measure value beyond generic Redis/Azure knowledge.
hardening_notes: Iteration 1 baselines were strong on generic Redis and Azure guidance, so these evals use review-style prompts with AMR-specific traps and anti-pattern checks.
The cache eval now explicitly tests Azure Managed Redis client safeguards, not just cache-stampede mechanics.
The Private Link and HA/DR evals now require details that generic Azure networking or reliability answers often miss.

Azure ecosystem evals test how AMR guidance composes with AKS, managed identity, Key Vault, App Configuration, Azure Monitor, Application Insights, Log Analytics, Event Grid, Service Bus, Azure Functions, Blob Storage, and Azure AI services.

evals.name: redis-cache-stampede
evals.prompt: Review this proposed Redis cache layer for a SQL-backed product catalog running on AKS with Azure Managed Redis. Current sketch: every HTTP request creates a new Redis client from REDIS_URL; local defaults are redis://<host>:6379 when env vars are missing; retryStrategy retries forever every 50 ms; hot SKU keys are product:{sku} with a fixed 15-minute TTL; cache misses acquire lock:{sku} with SETNX and later DEL without a token; if Redis times out, every pod immediately falls back to SQL. Rewrite the design as production-ready cache-aside guidance with key naming, expiration, stampede protection, and Azure Managed Redis client safeguards.
evals.expected_output: A practical cache-aside design for Azure Managed Redis that fixes unsafe client configuration, uses the service-returned endpoint and port with TLS, certificate validation, and startup config checks, sets explicit timeouts and bounded jittered retries, prevents hot-key stampedes with safe single-flight or stale-while-revalidate behavior, and avoids turning Redis failures into SQL overload.
expectations: Identifies the unsafe local Redis defaults and requires Azure Managed Redis production clients to use the service-returned host and port, TLS or rediss, certificate validation, and fail-fast validation for missing host, port, username, or credential settings; it may identify 10000 as the default but not the only valid port.
Requires a process-wide Redis client, connection multiplexer, or pool instead of creating and disconnecting clients on every HTTP request.
Specifies connection and socket timeouts plus bounded retries with exponential backoff, jitter, and an overall operation deadline; rejects infinite immediate retries.
Specifies namespaced and versioned cache keys with explicit TTLs and per-key jitter to avoid synchronized expiry.
Includes stampede protection such as single-flight refresh, stale-while-revalidate, or a Redis lock with a unique token, short TTL, and compare-and-delete release semantics.
Protects SQL during Redis incidents with request coalescing, stale serving, circuit breakers, concurrency limits, or other bulkhead behavior instead of letting every pod fall through at once.
Avoids unsafe production patterns such as KEYS, unbounded locks, no TTL, disabled TLS validation, plaintext redis:// endpoints, or unlimited retry loops.
anti_patterns: Suggests KEYS for production key discovery.
Uses a distributed lock without a TTL or unique token.
Keeps per-request Redis connections.
Keeps redis://, port 6379, disabled TLS, or disabled certificate validation for Azure Managed Redis production clients.
Uses an infinite retry loop or immediate retry storm during Redis outages.
Lets every application instance fall back to SQL at the same time when Redis is slow or unavailable.
Omits cache expiration guidance.
Treats Redis as the source of truth for the SQL-backed catalog without explaining consistency tradeoffs.

evals.name: redis-rag-tenant-isolation
evals.prompt: Critique and replace this Redis vector retrieval design for a multi-tenant support RAG system on Azure Managed Redis. Embeddings are 1536 dimensions. Each chunk has tenant, locale, product, ACL group, document id, page, section, source URI, document version, and knowledge-base version. The proposed design uses one global vector index, runs KNN across all chunks, filters tenant and ACL in application code after retrieval, stores only chunk text plus embedding in Redis, appends new chunks on every re-ingestion, and semantic-caches answers by normalized question only. Provide the corrected Redis schema, ingestion pattern, query pattern, and cache boundaries.
evals.expected_output: A Redis vector/RAG design that uses an AMR tier or cluster policy that supports RediSearch/vector modules, aligns the 1536-dimensional vector field and distance metric with the embedding model, stores filterable tenant/ACL/source metadata, enforces tenant and ACL filters inside every Redis vector query before context reaches the LLM, preserves stable citations, uses deterministic/idempotent ingestion, and scopes semantic cache entries by tenant, policy, model, prompt, and knowledge version.
expectations: Calls out that the AMR deployment must use a tier, modules, and cluster policy that support RediSearch/vector workloads before designing the index.
Defines a 1536-dimensional vector field and aligns the distance metric with the embedding model.
Stores tenant, locale, product, ACL group, document id, page, section, source URI, document version, and knowledge-base version as retrievable or filterable metadata alongside each vector.
Requires tenant and ACL filters inside every Redis vector query, before KNN results are passed to reranking or the LLM; rejects post-retrieval or post-generation authorization filtering.
Preserves stable source citation metadata so generated answers can cite document id, page, section, and source URI.
Mentions deterministic chunk IDs, content hashes, idempotent upserts, and stale-chunk deletion to avoid duplicate or orphaned chunks.
Scopes semantic answer cache keys and invalidation by tenant, ACL or policy boundary, embedding model, prompt template, and knowledge-base version.
anti_patterns: Runs vector search across all tenants and filters only after generation.
Filters tenant or ACL only in application code after Redis returns the nearest neighbors.
Drops source citation metadata from the index.
Ignores embedding dimensions or distance metric.
Caches RAG answers without tenant, policy, model, prompt, or knowledge-version boundaries.
Appends new chunks on every ingestion without deterministic IDs, idempotent upserts, or stale-chunk cleanup.
Ignores whether the selected Azure Managed Redis tier, modules, and cluster policy support vector search.

evals.name: amr-private-link-dns
evals.prompt: Review this proposed network plan for Azure Managed Redis. AKS runs in a spoke VNet, operators connect from a peered management VNet, and the security goal is no public data-plane access. The draft creates one private endpoint in a hub subnet, links the private DNS zone only to the hub, configures apps to connect to <cache>.privatelink.redis.azure.net, assumes VNet peering makes DNS work everywhere, leaves publicNetworkAccess enabled for admin break-glass, and sends all egress through Azure Firewall with no Redis-specific route validation. Identify what is wrong and provide the corrected production architecture and validation checklist.
evals.expected_output: An Azure Managed Redis Private Link plan that disables public network access, uses the redisEnterprise private endpoint connection, keeps clients on the resource-returned normal host name and database port with TLS, links the current cloud's AMR private DNS zone to every client VNet or forwards custom DNS correctly, validates DNS and TLS connectivity from each subnet, and accounts for subnet network policies, NSG/UDR/firewall routing, and /32 private endpoint route behavior.
expectations: Requires Private Link/private endpoint access and disabled publicNetworkAccess for the production data plane instead of relying on public access or IP allowlists.
Identifies Azure Managed Redis as Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise with private endpoint group id redisEnterprise.
Requires applications to connect to the resource-returned normal host name and database port with TLS, and explicitly rejects configuring clients to use a privatelink host name directly.

Uses the current cloud's AMR private DNS zone, identifies privatelink.redis.azure.net only as the public Azure example, and explains that it must resolve the normal cache hostname to the private endpoint IP.

Explains that VNet peering does not automatically provide DNS resolution; links the private DNS zone to the AKS spoke VNet, management VNet, and any resolver/shared-services VNet, or configures conditional forwarding through Azure DNS Private Resolver/custom DNS.
Calls out private endpoint subnet policy, NSG, UDR, firewall, and /32 route considerations that can block or bypass intended private endpoint traffic.

Includes validation from each participating network: nslookup or dig for the normal cache hostname returns the private endpoint IP, and a TLS Redis client test reaches the service-returned database port.
anti_patterns: Relies on public access plus IP allowlists as the main architecture.
Leaves publicNetworkAccess enabled for routine admin access in the production architecture.
Omits private DNS zone linking for peered VNets.
Assumes private endpoint DNS works automatically from every VNet.
Configures clients to connect to a privatelink hostname directly.
Uses the legacy Azure Cache for Redis resource type or group id instead of Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise and redisEnterprise.
Treats this as generic Redis networking without Azure Managed Redis controls.
Omits route, firewall, or subnet network policy validation.

evals.name: amr-ha-persistence-geo
evals.prompt: Review this pre-provisioning reliability proposal for an Azure Managed Redis dependency in checkout. The proposal says: start with the cheapest tier and add high availability later; enable persistence and active geo-replication on the same cache; use RDB files as point-in-time backups that can restore into a new cache in another region; add active geo-replication after launch if regional DR is required; assume geo-replication is synchronous with zero data loss; and let clients keep using a single endpoint during failover. Identify the mistakes and produce the corrected decision record for HA, zone redundancy, persistence/export backup, active geo-replication, client failover, and monitoring.
evals.expected_output: An AMR reliability decision record that separates HA/zone redundancy, persistence/export backup, and active geo-replication; calls out creation-time or hard-to-change choices such as tier/SKU, capacity, modules, cluster policy, networking, HA, and geo; explains that persistence requires HA, is not supported with active geo-replication, and is not a point-in-time or cross-cache restore feature; uses export to Blob for backups/migrations; treats active geo as active-active eventual consistency configured during provisioning with matching regional cache configuration; and includes client routing/failover and monitoring/runbook requirements.
expectations: Separates HA/zone redundancy, persistence/export backup, and active geo-replication as different reliability mechanisms with different failure modes and recovery objectives.

Calls out creation-time or difficult-to-change decisions such as tier/SKU, capacity, modules, Enterprise/cluster policy, region support, networking/private endpoints/DNS, HA, and active geo-replication topology.
States that Azure Managed Redis persistence requires high availability and is not supported with active geo-replication.
Explains that persistence is for node recovery and is not point-in-time backup or a way to restore persisted files into another cache; uses scheduled export to Blob storage for backups or migrations.

Explains that active geo-replication must be planned during provisioning, requires matching configuration across instances, supports active-active multi-region DR, and has eventual consistency rather than synchronous zero-data-loss semantics.
Includes client routing and failover behavior, including endpoint selection, retry deadlines, idempotency for writes, and testing of regional failover.

Includes monitoring and operational readiness checks for persistence/export status, geo-replication health/lag, memory/evictions, private endpoint/DNS health, restore drills, failover drills, and incident runbooks.
anti_patterns: Claims persistence alone provides regional DR.
Claims persistence provides point-in-time backups or cross-cache restore from persisted files.
Combines persistence and active geo-replication on the same Azure Managed Redis cache.
Claims active geo-replication can be bolted on after launch without provisioning-time planning.
Assumes active geo-replication is synchronous or guarantees zero data loss.
Ignores creation-time AMR choices.
Treats zone redundancy and active geo-replication as interchangeable.
Omits client behavior during failover.
Omits monitoring, restore drills, or failover drills.

evals.name: azure-aks-entra-keyvault-client
evals.prompt: Review this integration plan for a .NET API running on AKS that connects to Azure Managed Redis. The draft stores the AMR primary key in a Kubernetes Secret copied from Key Vault once a month, stores REDIS_URL as redis://cache:6379 in App Configuration, creates a Redis connection per request, gets a Microsoft Entra token once at startup but never refreshes it, and grants the AKS managed identity broad subscription Contributor so it can read everything. The team wants an Azure-native production pattern using AKS workload identity, App Configuration, Key Vault, Entra authentication, and AMR data access policies. What should the corrected application and configuration design include?
evals.expected_output: An Azure-native AMR client design for AKS that uses workload identity or managed identity, Microsoft Entra authentication with token refresh, least-privilege AMR data access policy assignment, Key Vault/App Configuration without hardcoded secrets, the service-returned host and port with TLS, singleton or pooled Redis clients, bounded timeouts/retries, and observability for authentication and connection failures.
expectations: Replaces static AMR access keys in Kubernetes Secrets with Microsoft Entra authentication using AKS workload identity or managed identity, keeping access keys disabled unless a documented client limitation requires them.
Specifies least-privilege AMR data-plane access through data access policies or scoped role assignment for the AKS workload identity rather than broad subscription Contributor.
Uses Azure App Configuration for non-secret endpoint/settings and Key Vault references or Key Vault only for exceptional secrets; rejects hardcoded connection strings and stale copied secrets.

Requires clients to use the service-returned Azure Managed Redis host and port with TLS or rediss and certificate validation, not redis://cache:6379; it may identify 10000 as the default without rejecting another returned port.
Requires a singleton Redis client, connection multiplexer, or pool coordinated with token refresh instead of creating clients per request.
Explains that Entra tokens expire and must be refreshed before expiry so pooled connections reconnect or re-authenticate with fresh tokens.
Includes bounded connection/socket timeouts, bounded retries with jitter, startup config validation, and logging/metrics for auth failures, connection failures, token refresh, and Redis latency.
anti_patterns: Keeps AMR primary keys as the normal AKS authentication path.
Grants broad subscription Contributor to the application identity.
Copies secrets from Key Vault into Kubernetes and relies on manual monthly rotation as the primary control.
Uses redis://, port 6379, plaintext traffic, disabled certificate validation, or local Redis defaults in production.
Gets an Entra token once at startup for a long-running service and never refreshes it.
Creates Redis clients per HTTP request.
Omits observability for authentication or connection failures.

evals.name: azure-monitor-appinsights-loganalytics
evals.prompt: Review this observability plan for Azure Managed Redis backing an AKS checkout service and an App Service admin portal. The draft says the team will watch the Azure portal metrics manually, leave diagnostic settings off to reduce cost, rely on Application Insights request failures only, and add alerts after the first outage. They also use Private Link, Entra authentication, and active geo-replication. Create the corrected Azure Monitor, Log Analytics, Application Insights, alerting, dashboard, and runbook plan.
evals.expected_output: An Azure observability plan that discovers and enables the metric and diagnostic-log categories supported by the deployed AMR resource, routes available signals to Log Analytics, correlates application dependency telemetry from AKS/App Service through Application Insights, defines alert baselines/action groups/runbooks before launch, covers Private Link/DNS and Entra auth failures, includes supported active-geo replication status or lag signals where used, and uses dashboards/workbooks/KQL for investigation.
expectations: Queries the Azure Monitor categories and metric definitions supported by the deployed AMR resource/API version, enables the available metric and connection/audit log signals before launch, and routes them to a Log Analytics workspace or equivalent approved destination without inventing unsupported category names.

Defines actionable Azure Monitor alerts with action groups and runbook links for memory pressure, server load or CPU, latency, evictions, connected clients, connection errors, authentication failures, and availability.
Includes alerts on supported active geo-replication status or lag signals and regional dependency checks when active geo-replication is enabled.
Includes Private Link, private DNS, firewall, and resolver health signals or validation so network failures are not hidden behind generic app errors.
Uses Application Insights dependency telemetry from AKS and App Service to correlate Redis latency/errors with request failures and deployment changes.
Uses Log Analytics queries, Azure Workbooks, dashboards, or saved KQL views for historical investigation across AMR, application, network, and identity signals.
Baselines thresholds from load testing or SLOs before production and commits to tuning after launch rather than waiting for the first outage.
anti_patterns: Relies only on manual Azure portal metric viewing.
Leaves diagnostic settings disabled for production.
Adds alerts only after an outage.
Uses Application Insights request failures without Redis dependency correlation.
Omits available connection/audit or authentication-failure visibility when Entra authentication is used.
Omits geo-replication health when active geo-replication is part of the architecture.
Omits action groups, owners, or runbook links.

evals.name: azure-event-driven-cache-invalidation
evals.prompt: Review this Azure event-driven cache invalidation design for Azure Managed Redis. Product changes originate in Azure SQL and are published to Event Grid, then Azure Functions invalidates Redis keys. The draft handler receives an event, runs KEYS product:* and DEL for every match, ignores event version/order, has no idempotency key, uses a Redis access key in app settings, retries forever on failure, and has no dead-letter or replay plan. Some downstream consumers also need a durable stream of invalidation events. Provide a safer design using Azure Event Grid or Service Bus, Azure Functions, Redis key conventions, AMR client safety, and reliable downstream processing.
evals.expected_output: An Azure event-driven invalidation design that avoids broad key scans, invalidates deterministic versioned keys, handles out-of-order and duplicate events idempotently, uses Event Grid or Service Bus retry/dead-letter semantics intentionally, connects to AMR with Entra/TLS/reused clients/timeouts/bounded retries, and uses Redis Streams or Service Bus topics for durable downstream replay where needed.
expectations: Rejects KEYS product:* and broad deletes in production; uses deterministic namespaced/versioned keys or maintains explicit per-entity index keys for targeted invalidation.
Handles duplicate, out-of-order, and replayed Azure events with idempotency keys, entity version or updated_at checks, and safe no-op behavior for stale events.
Chooses Event Grid for lightweight event notification or Service Bus topics/queues when ordering, sessions, dead-lettering, replay, or stronger delivery controls are required; explains the tradeoff.
Defines Azure Functions retry, poison-message, dead-letter, and replay behavior without infinite retry loops.

Uses Azure Managed Redis client safeguards: Entra or managed identity where supported, the service-returned host and port with TLS, singleton/pool reuse, certificate validation, timeouts, bounded retries, and secretless configuration where possible.
Uses Redis Streams with consumer groups or Azure Service Bus topics for downstream consumers that need durable replay and acknowledgments rather than Redis Pub/Sub.
Includes observability through Application Insights/Azure Monitor for event lag, handler failures, Redis latency/errors, dead-letter counts, and invalidation volume.
anti_patterns: Uses KEYS or FLUSHDB for production invalidation.
Deletes cache entries without considering event version, ordering, duplicate delivery, or idempotency.
Uses infinite retries in Azure Functions or Redis client code.
Stores Redis access keys in function app settings as the preferred production authentication path.
Uses Redis Pub/Sub for critical invalidation events that require replay or acknowledgments.
Omits dead-letter, poison-message, or replay handling.
Omits monitoring for invalidation lag or failure rates.

evals.name: azure-ai-blob-rag-ingestion
evals.prompt: Design a production RAG ingestion and retrieval pipeline on Azure using Azure Blob Storage for source documents, Event Grid for blob-change notifications, Azure Functions or Azure Container Apps jobs for chunking, Azure OpenAI or Azure AI Foundry for embeddings, and Azure Managed Redis for vector search. The draft indexes every blob event immediately with a random Redis key, stores only chunk text and embedding, mixes embedding models in the same index, caches answers by question text only, and has no tenant, document version, source URI, page, or content hash metadata. It also uses public AMR access and access keys from app settings. Provide the corrected Azure ecosystem design.
evals.expected_output: An Azure RAG pipeline that uses Event Grid/Blob events safely, idempotent chunking with content hashes and document versions, Azure AI embeddings with one model/dimension per Redis index, AMR vector schema with tenant/source/citation metadata, tenant/ACL filters in Redis queries, semantic cache boundaries, managed identity or Entra authentication, Private Link/TLS, and observability across Blob, Functions/ACA, Azure AI, and AMR.
expectations: Uses Blob Storage events through Event Grid as triggers but makes ingestion idempotent with content hashes, deterministic chunk IDs, document version or ETag, and stale-chunk cleanup.
Keeps one embedding model, dimension, and distance metric contract per Redis vector index; creates a new index or re-embeds when the Azure AI embedding model changes.
Stores tenant, ACL or policy boundary, source URI, document id, document version, page, section, content hash, embedding model, and knowledge-base version with each vector for filtering and citation.
Requires tenant and ACL filters inside every Redis vector query before retrieved context reaches reranking or the LLM.
Scopes semantic answer cache entries by tenant, ACL or policy boundary, Azure AI model, prompt version, embedding model, and knowledge-base version rather than by question text only.

Uses Azure Managed Redis production connectivity: Private Link where required, service-returned host and port, TLS/cert validation, Entra or managed identity authentication where supported, and no public access-key-in-app-settings default.

Includes operational visibility across Azure Blob/Event Grid, Functions or Container Apps, Azure AI embedding calls, AMR indexing/query latency, failures, retries, dead letters, and cost/throughput limits.
anti_patterns: Uses random Redis vector keys on every blob event without idempotency.
Mixes embedding models or dimensions in the same Redis vector index.
Stores only chunk text and embedding with no source/citation or authorization metadata.
Filters tenant or ACL only after retrieval or generation.
Caches RAG answers by question text only.
Uses public AMR access or Redis access keys in app settings as the default production connection pattern.
Omits dead-letter, retry, rate-limit, or observability design for Blob/Event Grid/Azure AI/AMR failures.

evals.name: amr-sizing-from-workload-metrics
evals.prompt: Review this Azure Managed Redis sizing recommendation. The team wants to pick Balanced B10 because it roughly matches their old cache label and says they can resize later. They have 10 days of metrics: peak used memory 18 GB, P95 used memory 14 GB, Server Load often 78-85%, 55K connected clients at peak, high read bandwidth, and they also need RedisJSON and RediSearch. They have not checked region availability or preview status. Produce the corrected AMR tier/SKU decision process and what should be validated before provisioning.
evals.expected_output: A metric-based AMR sizing process that uses peak/P95 memory, Server Load, connected clients, bandwidth, module needs, regional availability, and preview status instead of source SKU labels; compares usable memory to target capacity; considers X-series for compute/client pressure, B-series for balanced load, M-series for memory-heavy workloads, and Flash only for very large tiered-storage cases; and treats modules, cluster policy, HA, networking, diagnostics, and active geo as creation-time or hard-to-change decisions.
expectations: Rejects choosing an AMR SKU only because it resembles an older/source cache label or because it is the smallest acceptable-looking tier.
Uses peak and P95 used memory, Server Load or CPU pressure, connected clients, read/write bandwidth, latency targets, and module requirements as sizing inputs.
Compares usable memory and capacity rather than only advertised SKU size, and recommends sizing to cover peak used memory.
Considers Compute Optimized X-series when server load, command complexity, bandwidth, or client count are high relative to memory.
Explains when Memory Optimized, Balanced, Compute Optimized, and Flash Optimized tiers are appropriate.
Requires validation of region availability, preview SKU status, module support, cluster policy, HA, networking, diagnostics, and active geo needs before provisioning.
Avoids customer-facing AMR shard-count language and describes AMR scale in terms of tier, SKU, capacity, and cluster policy.
anti_patterns: Maps directly from a source SKU label without using workload metrics.
Ignores Server Load, connected clients, or bandwidth when memory appears sufficient.
Recommends the smallest SKU while dismissing creation-time or hard-to-change choices.
Uses AMR shard count as a customer sizing control.
Omits module, cluster policy, region availability, or preview-status validation.

evals.name: amr-native-iac-arm-bicep-terraform
evals.prompt: Generate guidance for a production Azure Managed Redis IaC module that must support ARM, Bicep, and Terraform. The draft creates one generic Redis resource, leaves database settings implicit, omits clusteringPolicy, uses public access by default, creates no private endpoint DNS zone group, and tells apps to infer the port. Provide the corrected native AMR IaC resource shape, required database/default-database settings, Private Link/DNS settings, and validation steps.
evals.expected_output: Native AMR IaC guidance that models ARM/Bicep as Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise plus Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise/databases named default, uses Terraform azurerm_managed_redis with default_database, explicitly configures the database port (10000 by default), clientProtocol, clusteringPolicy, evictionPolicy, modules, and persistence where applicable, disables public access for production Private Link, uses private endpoint subresource redisEnterprise and the current cloud's AMR private DNS zone, returns the resulting host and port to applications, and validates with what-if or terraform validate/plan.
expectations: For ARM/Bicep, models the AMR cluster and the default database as separate resources with the database depending on the cluster.
For Terraform, uses azurerm_managed_redis with sku_name, public_network_access, high_availability_enabled, and a default_database block.

Places data-plane settings such as the configured port (10000 by default), clientProtocol, clusteringPolicy, evictionPolicy, modules, persistence, and geo-replication on the database/default_database configuration.

Uses Private Link for production, disables public network access, uses private endpoint group/subresource redisEnterprise, and uses the current cloud's AMR private DNS zone (privatelink.redis.azure.net only as the public-Azure example).
Returns the normal resource host name and configured database port to clients rather than reconstructing a public-cloud hostname or using a privatelink hostname.
Includes diagnostic settings, alerts, identity/access policy assignments, and parameterized creation-time decisions in the IaC module.
Requires preflight validation such as ARM/Bicep what-if or terraform validate and terraform plan.
anti_patterns: Creates a single generic Redis resource without a default database configuration.
Omits clusteringPolicy or relies on provider defaults.
Leaves production public network access enabled without a justified exception.
Uses the wrong private endpoint group/subresource or private DNS zone.
Tells application clients to connect to a privatelink hostname directly.
Omits validation before deployment.

evals.name: redis-tenant-key-and-cluster-design
evals.prompt: Review this Redis application design for Azure Managed Redis. The app was copied from a design that uses Redis database indexes with SELECT for tenant separation, and it also runs MGET and DEL batches over keys like tenantA:user:1:cart and tenantA:user:1:totals. The infrastructure team is choosing between NoCluster, OSSCluster, and EnterpriseCluster policies. One engineer says hash tags are required for every multi-key command under every policy; another says they are never needed. Recommend portable tenant key naming and explain the documented cross-slot behavior and client assumptions for these policies.
evals.expected_output: A Redis application design that prefers explicit key prefixes and centralized key builders over database indexes as a portable tenant-separation approach; explains that NoCluster is unsharded and has no slot-based restriction, OSSCluster requires every multi-key command's keys to map to the same hash slot, and EnterpriseCluster permits only a documented subset of multi-key commands (DEL, MSET, MGET, EXISTS, UNLINK, TOUCH) across slots; recommends hash tags when related keys must be co-located without claiming they are required for every EnterpriseCluster command; warns about CROSSSLOT where applicable; and selects a Redis Cluster-aware client for OSSCluster while using a single-endpoint client for EnterpriseCluster or NoCluster.
expectations: Prefers explicit, consistently built key prefixes over Redis database indexes for portable tenant, environment, and workload separation.
Explains that NoCluster is unsharded and has no slot-based restriction for multi-key commands.
Explains that OSSCluster requires keys used by a multi-key command to map to the same hash slot.
Identifies DEL, MSET, MGET, EXISTS, UNLINK, and TOUCH as the documented EnterpriseCluster commands that can operate across slots.
Recommends hash tags to co-locate related keys when required, without claiming every EnterpriseCluster multi-key command needs them.
Explains CROSSSLOT risk for commands whose keys must share a slot.
Uses a Redis Cluster-aware client for OSSCluster and a single-endpoint client for EnterpriseCluster or NoCluster.
Recommends prefix-scoped key scans and batched deletion for tenant-scoped cleanup.
anti_patterns: Claims hash tags are mandatory for every multi-key command under EnterpriseCluster, ignoring its documented cross-slot command subset.
Claims hash tags are never needed for clustered multi-key operations.
Recommends SELECT or Redis database indexes as the portable tenant-separation design instead of key prefixes.
Chooses OSSCluster while assuming a non-cluster-aware client will work unchanged.
Ignores CROSSSLOT risk when a command's keys must share a slot.

evals.name: amr-tenant-isolation-infrastructure
evals.prompt: Review this Azure Managed Redis infrastructure plan. A platform team provisions one Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise/databases resource named default and plans to put multiple tenants in it. The team needs strong separation for regulated tenants. Explain what key prefixes can provide, how data access permissions should be scoped, and when separate caches are the appropriate isolation boundary. Do not infer Redis logical-database behavior from the resource layout.
evals.expected_output: Infrastructure guidance that distinguishes key prefixes as an application-level naming and organization technique from access control; recommends scoped identities and data access permissions for restricting users or applications; and recommends separate Azure Managed Redis caches when the requirement is a stronger resource-level tenant boundary. It does not infer logical-database behavior from the single default database resource.
expectations: Explains that key prefixes provide application-level naming separation, not access control.
Recommends scoped identities and data access permissions to restrict tenant access.
Recommends a separate AMR cache when a stronger resource-level tenant isolation boundary is required.
Does not infer logical-database behavior from the Microsoft.Cache/redisEnterprise/databases/default resource.
Avoids recommending Redis database indexes as a security boundary.
anti_patterns: Treats key prefixes alone as an access-control or hard-isolation boundary.
Treats the single default database resource as proof of logical-database behavior.
Recommends Redis database indexes as a security boundary.
Omits scoped access permissions when discussing tenant access.
Omits separate caches when the requirement is stronger resource-level isolation.

evals.name: redis-service-returned-port-no-harm
evals.prompt: Generate a production Python client configuration for an Azure Managed Redis database whose deployment output is hostName=orders-cache.example.internal and port=13000. A teammate wants to replace the port with 10000 and fail startup whenever REDIS_PORT is not 10000 because that is the usual AMR port. Review that proposal and provide the corrected client setup. Do not connect to Azure.
evals.expected_output: A client setup that preserves the service-returned host name and port 13000, enables TLS with certificate validation, validates that configuration is present and well-formed without rejecting a valid non-default port, and explains that 10000 is a common AMR database port rather than a universal constant.
expectations: Uses orders-cache.example.internal and port 13000 from deployment configuration rather than replacing either value.
Does not throw, fail startup, or warn merely because the service-returned port differs from 10000.
Identifies 10000 as a common AMR database port rather than a universal constant.
Enables TLS or rediss with certificate validation and validates required configuration at startup.
Uses a reusable client or pool with explicit timeouts and bounded retry behavior.
anti_patterns: Hardcodes port 10000 or overwrites the supplied port 13000.
Rejects every port other than 10000.
Reconstructs a public-Azure hostname instead of using orders-cache.example.internal.
Uses port 6380, port 6379, plaintext redis, or disabled certificate validation.
Hardcodes a direct-node or redirect port instead of following service topology.

evals.name: amr-minimum-tls-property
evals.prompt: Review this Azure Managed Redis Bicep proposal: minimumTlsVersion is set to '1.3' and the default database clientProtocol is Plaintext because the team assumes TLS 1.3 is the newest allowed minimum. Provide the corrected production settings and explain the distinction between the control-plane minimum-version property and the TLS protocol a client may negotiate. Do not deploy.
evals.expected_output: Infrastructure guidance that sets minimumTlsVersion to 1.2, keeps clientProtocol encrypted, requires client certificate validation, explains that 1.3 is not an accepted minimumTlsVersion value, and treats negotiated wire-protocol support as a separate capability without making unsupported claims about when the setting can be changed.
expectations: Sets or recommends minimumTlsVersion '1.2' as the accepted control-plane value.
Rejects minimumTlsVersion '1.3' rather than presenting it as a stronger valid setting.
Keeps clientProtocol encrypted and requires TLS with certificate validation.
Distinguishes the control-plane minimum-version property from the protocol version a client may negotiate.
Avoids claiming that minimumTlsVersion is immutable or can only be set at creation.
anti_patterns: Sets minimumTlsVersion to 1.3.
Claims the control plane accepts either 1.2 or 1.3 for minimumTlsVersion.
Leaves clientProtocol as Plaintext.
Disables certificate validation.
Conflates a possible wire-level TLS negotiation with the allowed IaC property value.

evals.name: redisjson-osscluster-policy
evals.prompt: Review an Azure Managed Redis design that uses OSSCluster with the RedisJSON module but does not enable Search. One reviewer claims RedisJSON and Search both require EnterpriseCluster. The team may add vector search later and may eventually use active geo-replication. Based only on publicly documented Azure Managed Redis guidance, assess each claim, distinguish documented requirements from assumptions, and explain what must change if Search or geo is added. Do not rely on internal implementation details or cite URLs.
evals.expected_output: Public-documentation-grounded guidance that states the public module documentation requires EnterpriseCluster and NoEviction for RediSearch and does not establish whether RedisJSON alone is compatible with OSSCluster; it neither asserts nor rejects that combination without a public compatibility source. Vector search uses RediSearch and therefore needs those settings and module selection at creation. Active geo supports only RediSearch and RedisJSON, requires high availability and matching member configuration, and does not support Flash Optimized. EnterpriseCluster is not a universal active-geo requirement.
expectations: States that public module guidance does not establish RedisJSON compatibility or incompatibility with OSSCluster; does not infer either from the Search restriction and recommends verifying the exact combination against a public service compatibility reference before recommending it.
States that RediSearch requires EnterpriseCluster and NoEviction, and is incompatible with OSSCluster.
States that vector search uses RediSearch and recommends selecting the module and required policy at creation because modules cannot be added to an existing instance.
States that active geo-replication supports only RediSearch and RedisJSON, requires high availability and matching member configuration, and does not support Flash Optimized.
Does not claim active geo-replication universally requires EnterpriseCluster; distinguishes the documented Search requirement from the unestablished RedisJSON/OSSCluster combination.
anti_patterns: States that RedisJSON is confirmed supported with OSSCluster solely from the current public module guidance.
States that RedisJSON requires EnterpriseCluster as a documented requirement based only on Search's policy restriction.
Claims RediSearch is supported with OSSCluster or recommends Search without NoEviction.
Treats all Redis modules as supported with active geo-replication.
Claims active geo-replication always requires EnterpriseCluster, regardless of module choice.
Says modules can be added to an existing instance or ignores the documented tier and geo restrictions.

evals.name: amr-automatic-zone-redundancy
evals.prompt: Review this Azure Managed Redis deployment plan. The team wants zone redundancy, but assumes it must choose and submit specific availability-zone IDs. It is considering disabling high availability if it cannot choose the zones itself. Explain the documented way to get zone redundancy and what the team should verify before deployment. Do not deploy.
evals.expected_output: Guidance that enables high availability and deploys the cache in a region that supports availability zones; explains that, in supported regions, Azure Managed Redis automatically distributes cache nodes across zones with no additional zone configuration; and does not promise zone redundancy in regions without availability zones.
expectations: Recommends the high availability configuration for zone redundancy.
States that in regions with availability zones, Azure Managed Redis automatically distributes nodes across zones without requiring the customer to select zone IDs.
States that high availability without availability-zone support in the region does not provide cross-zone placement.
Recommends validating both Azure Managed Redis availability and availability-zone support in the target region.
Does not recommend disabling high availability merely because explicit zone selection is unavailable.
anti_patterns: Claims the customer must select and submit explicit zone IDs to obtain AMR zone redundancy.
Promises zone redundancy in a region that does not support availability zones.
Recommends disabling high availability because the customer cannot choose specific zones.
Imports Azure Cache for Redis zone-selection requirements into Azure Managed Redis guidance.
Ignores regional support for availability zones.

evals.name: redis-amr-service-managed-memory
evals.prompt: Review this Azure Managed Redis capacity plan. The team targets 20 GB of data, chooses the allkeys-lru eviction policy, and assumes that eviction means writes can never fail. Explain how to choose capacity, configure eviction, and monitor memory using documented Azure Managed Redis guidance. Do not connect to a cache.
evals.expected_output: Guidance that sizes the cache using the workload's dataset and the selected SKU's capacity, chooses an eviction policy that fits the application's key-retention needs, and monitors Used Memory Percentage with alerts and scaling considerations. It accounts for the documented behavior of the Used Memory metric and does not promise that eviction eliminates the need for capacity planning or monitoring.
expectations: Chooses cache capacity based on the workload's dataset size and the selected SKU's memory capacity, rather than a client-owned fixed memory limit.
Chooses an eviction policy based on which keys should be eligible for eviction and uses the Azure Managed Redis resource configuration for that setting.
Explains that Used Memory includes primary and replica shards when high availability is enabled, while the SKU memory limit already accounts for replication.
Recommends monitoring Used Memory Percentage and alerting before capacity pressure; identifies scaling as an option when usage remains high.
Does not claim that eviction removes the need to size and monitor the cache.
anti_patterns: Treats the configured dataset target as a guaranteed amount of available memory independent of SKU.
Chooses an eviction policy without considering which keys are eligible for eviction.
Misreads the Used Memory metric as excluding high-availability replicas.
Promises that an eviction policy eliminates capacity planning or monitoring.
Omits SKU capacity, Used Memory Percentage monitoring, or alerting.

evals.name: amr-geo-effective-cardinality
evals.prompt: A team has five caches in a pure Azure Managed Redis active geo-replication group and wants to add a sixth as permanent capacity, citing a six-member group they saw during an ACRE-to-AMR migration. Using only publicly documented behavior, review the proposal: state the documented maximum group size, whether a permanent sixth member is supported, and what must be verified before changing membership. Do not call Azure and do not speculate about internal enforcement mechanisms.
evals.expected_output: Public-documentation-grounded guidance that states the documented maximum active geo-replication group size is five, concludes a permanent sixth member is not supported, declines to treat a transient state observed during a migration as supported permanent capacity, and recommends checking current public guidance and compatible member configuration before changing membership - without asserting internal engine or enforcement details.
expectations: States that the documented maximum active geo-replication group size is five.
Concludes that a permanent sixth member is not supported and rejects the proposal.
Declines to treat a one-off or transient state observed during a migration as evidence of supported permanent capacity.
Requires planning any membership change as a supported, validated workflow with compatible member configuration (matching SKU, modules, and policies).
Stays within publicly documented behavior and does not assert internal engine limits, enforcement mechanisms, or named internal thresholds.
anti_patterns: Claims an AMR geo group supports six or more permanent members.
Treats an undocumented or transient migration state as supported permanent capacity.
Explains the limit by internal enforcement mechanism, configuration source, or a named internal threshold rather than documented behavior.
Recommends changing membership without confirming the current documented limit or member compatibility.
Presents the limit as a fixed engine constant with no direction to verify current documentation.
